takeaways: Coronary vasospasm is reversible coronary artery narrowing from smooth muscle constriction, classically linked to Prinzmetal angina.
Episodes may occur at rest, often at night, and can produce transient ST elevation on ECG.
Functional ischemia can exist with angiographically mild or normal epicardial arteries.
Triggers include smoking, stimulants, and certain medications in teaching lists.
Diagnosis may require provocative testing in specialty settings, not a self-test topic.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Coronary vasospasm narrows the vessel lumen through intense smooth muscle contraction rather than fixed atherosclerotic plaque. When flow drops below myocardial demand, ischemia and pain result, sometimes with arrhythmia.
Prinzmetal (variant) angina historically described rest angina with ST elevation that resolves as spasm relaxes.
Vasospasm coexists with atherosclerosis in some patients; stenosis lowers flow reserve, making spasm more symptomatic.
Misconception: young smokers with normal angiograms cannot have serious ischemia-vasospasm disproves that.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and hypercontractile smooth muscle contribute in models. Smoking is a major preventable contributor in educational materials.
Transmural ischemia during spasm can mimic STEMI on ECG until resolution-differentiation requires clinical correlation and serial ECG.
Multivessel spasm or malignant arrhythmia during spasm explains rare sudden events in case reports.
Microvascular angina may overlap when epicardial spasm is absent but microvascular constriction occurs.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Rest chest pain, especially nocturnal or early morning, with cyclical ST changes supports teaching diagnoses. Exercise may be less triggering than in fixed stenosis, though overlap exists.
Symptoms can include syncope or palpitations when ischemia provokes arrhythmia.
Atypical chest pain workups sometimes miss vasospasm if only exercise stress is performed.
Patient-reported triggers (cold exposure, stress) are clues, not proof.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Coronary angiography with intracoronary acetylcholine or ergonovine provocative testing is used in research and expert centers with safety protocols.
Ambulatory ECG may capture transient ST changes during spontaneous pain.
Non-invasive coronary CT may exclude fixed disease before functional testing emphasis.
Calcium channel blockers and nitrates appear in guideline discussions for treatment-specific prescribing is clinician role.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Contrast vasospasm with fixed stenosis using timing and ECG features in case vignettes.
List modifiable triggers to counsel about in general education (smoking cessation themes).
Explain why exercise stress tests may be falsely reassuring.
Study MINOCA workups where vasospasm enters differential after non-obstructive angiography.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Coronary vasospasm highlights functional ischemia-dynamic luminal change without severe fixed plaque.
Rest pain and transient ST elevation are pedagogical clues; confirmation often needs specialized testing.
Cardily separates mechanism learning from provocative testing decisions made by experienced teams.

takeaways: Myocardial bridging occurs when a coronary artery segment tunnels through myocardium, potentially compressed in systole.
It is common at autopsy yet often asymptomatic-symptom attribution requires careful integration.
Debate continues over when bridging causes ischemia versus incidental finding on CTA.
Intravascular imaging and fractional flow reserve during dobutamine may clarify hemodynamic significance in expert hands.
Treatment spans medical therapy to surgical unroofing in selected refractory cases-specialist domain.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: A myocardial bridge is an anatomic variant where a coronary artery (often the mid left anterior descending) dives into the myocardium instead of remaining on the epicardial surface. Systolic muscle contraction may pinch the segment, affecting flow more in diastole-dominated coronary perfusion paradoxically in some models.
Why it matters educationally: CTA and angiography reports frequently mention bridging in young patients with chest pain, creating counseling challenges.
Bridging differs from anomalous origins and SCAD-students sort anatomy labels precisely.
Misconception: any bridge on a report explains all symptoms. Many bridges are benign.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Systolic compression visible on angiography (‘milking’) is a classic image. Hemodynamic significance depends on depth, length, and associated endothelial dysfunction or vasospasm.
Tachycardia shortens diastole, potentially worsening flow through a bridged segment in theory.
Associated atherosclerosis within the bridged segment occurs because turbulence and shear alter wall biology.
Arrhythmia and microvascular dysfunction may coexist, muddying causality.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate bridging from obstructive CAD, vasospasm, HCM, and anxiety-related chest pain using integrated testing.
Athletes with bridging present in sports cardiology debates-restriction is not automatic.
Symptoms resembling angina with normal epicardial stenosis should prompt functional evaluation rather than dismissal.
Student drill: What additional data would convince you bridging is symptomatic versus incidental?

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Beta blockers and rate control appear in case series to prolong diastole conceptually. Nitrates may worsen bridging in some teaching examples-an important paradox to remember.
Surgical myotomy or bypass is rare for severe confirmed cases.
Stenting bridged segments historically caused complications; contemporary caution persists.
Shared decision-making emphasizes uncertainty when evidence is case-based.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Read imaging reports critically-depth and length descriptors vary by modality.
Discuss psychological impact of ‘anatomic abnormality’ labels on active adults.
Explore research on combined vasospasm and bridging phenotypes.
Practice explaining why autopsy prevalence exceeds symptomatic prevalence.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Myocardial bridging teaches humility about incidental anatomy on modern imaging. Compression in systole may or may not translate to ischemia.
Differential thinking and functional testing separate benign variants from actionable ones in specialty pathways.
Cardily clarifies debates; invasive plans belong where imaging and physiology align with symptoms.

takeaways: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and no primary left heart or lung parenchymal cause.
WHO Group 1 in classification schemes; distinct from Group 2 (left heart) and Group 3 (lung disease).
Symptoms are nonspecific-dyspnea, fatigue, syncope-often delaying diagnosis until advanced.
Right heart catheterization is required for formal hemodynamic definition in guidelines.
Targeted vasodilator therapies exist for PAH but are not interchangeable with general pulmonary hypertension labels.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: PAH is a hemodynamic diagnosis: mean pulmonary artery pressure above guideline thresholds with normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, after excluding other World Health Organization groups.
Why classification literacy matters: giving PAH-specific drugs to Group 2 pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease can harm-teaching emphasizes correct grouping before therapy vocabulary.
Idiopathic, heritable, drug-associated, and connective tissue disease-associated subtypes appear in registries.
Misconception: echo-estimated PA pressure alone diagnoses PAH. Catheterization confirms.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Progressive remodeling of small pulmonary arterioles increases resistance; right ventricle hypertrophies then fails, producing systemic congestion.
Endothelial dysfunction, imbalance of vasoconstrictors and vasodilators, and proliferation mirror vascular biology themes from systemic hypertension but in the pulmonary circuit.
Exercise imposes rising cardiac output against fixed resistance-explaining exertional syncope as ominous sign.
Natural history without treatment historically led to RV failure; modern therapies modify trajectories in trials learners review qualitatively.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate PAH from chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (Group 4), which may be surgical or interventional in selected cases.
Left heart failure with preserved EF can elevate pulmonary pressures with normal wedge only in specific hemodynamic profiles-expert interpretation required.
Lung disease and hypoxia (Group 3) dominate epidemiologically; PAH is rarer but treatment-specific.
Portopulmonary hypertension in liver disease is a specialized subset.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: PAH therapies include endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin pathway agents, and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators-learn classes, not personal regimens.
Combination therapy strategies evolve with trial data; humility about rapid guideline change is warranted.
Supportive care includes diuretics for RV failure, oxygen when indicated, and supervised rehabilitation where safe.
Transplant evaluation enters advanced disease discussions.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Draw WHO Group 1-5 table from memory with one example each.
Explain why vasodilator challenge during cath is specialized testing.
Study connective tissue disease screening themes in new PAH diagnoses.
Follow registry outcomes language without repeating outdated survival numbers.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: PAH demands hemodynamic classification literacy before drug names make sense. Pre-capillary resistance elevation drives RV failure over time.
Differential diagnosis excludes left heart, lung, and thromboembolic explanations for pulmonary hypertension.
Cardily teaches structure; PAH centers manage complex vasoactive regimens and clinical trials access.

takeaways: Hemorrhagic stroke involves bleeding into brain parenchyma (intracerebral) or subarachnoid space, distinct from ischemic infarction.
Hypertensive arteriopathy and cerebral amyloid angiopathy are common teaching associations in older adults.
Anticoagulation and antiplatelet use increase bleeding risk-cardiology learners intersect here.
Neuroimaging non-contrast CT usually detects acute blood; ischemic therapies are contraindicated when hemorrhage present.
Stroke is not one disease-cardiovascular care must respect subtype before echo-driven embolic workups dominate.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Hemorrhagic stroke accounts for a minority of strokes globally but carries high mortality and morbidity. Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) bleeds into brain tissue; subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) often arises from ruptured saccular aneurysms with thunderclap headache.
Educational framing: the same ‘stroke’ word covers opposite vascular events-clot versus bleed-requiring immediate imaging differentiation.
Cardiology overlap peaks with ICH during anticoagulation for AF or mechanical valves, and when hypertensive heart disease reflects long-standing pressure load.
Misconception: small hemorrhages always produce mild deficits-location determines impact.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Chronic hypertension lipohyalinosis weakens small penetrating arteries, predisposing to basal ganglia or thalamic ICH in classic teaching.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhages in elderly, sometimes recurrent.
Anticoagulant-associated ICH expands hematoma more readily; reversal agents are protocol topics in hospitals.
Aneurysmal SAH triggers vasospasm days later, a secondary injury phase learners catalog.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Sudden focal deficit, decreased consciousness, headache, vomiting, and seizure may occur with ICH. SAH presents with abrupt maximal headache, meningismus, and altered mentation.
Blood pressure is often elevated acutely-whether to lower aggressively is managed per neurology protocols, not self-directed.
Neurologic exam localizes deficit; unlike ischemic stroke, thrombolysis is excluded when blood is present.
Student drill: Why must AF patients with sudden headache get CT before assuming embolic ischemia?

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Non-contrast head CT is first-line emergently. MRI sensitive for small bleeds later. Vascular imaging evaluates aneurysm, AVM, or cavernoma when appropriate.
Labs include coagulation studies, platelet function when relevant, and toxicology if suspected.
Echocardiography may still occur for long-term management planning but does not replace neuro diagnosis.
Blood pressure management, ICP control, and surgical evacuation decisions are neurosurgical territory.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Build a side-by-side ischemic versus hemorrhagic stroke algorithm ending at CT.
List antithrombotic factors increasing ICH risk conceptually.
Study restart timing of anticoagulation after ICH as evolving evidence area without quoting timelines as rules.
Connect hypertensive heart disease prevention to brain hemorrhage risk reduction themes.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Hemorrhagic stroke education insists stroke subtyping precedes cardiac embolic narratives. Blood on CT redirects the entire pathway.
Hypertension and antithrombotic therapy bridge cardiology and neurology; respectful interdisciplinary language helps families.
Cardily contrasts mechanisms; hyperacute care stays with stroke teams and imaging-first protocols.

takeaways: Hypertension is sustained elevation of arterial blood pressure, a major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor.
Pressure load damages endothelium, stiffens arteries, promotes LV hypertrophy, and accelerates atherosclerosis.
It is often asymptomatic-earning the ‘silent killer’ label in public health education.
Diagnosis requires repeated standardized measurements, not single readings.
Treatment categories span lifestyle and pharmacologic classes at guideline level; individualization is clinical.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Hypertension describes blood pressure above thresholds defined by guideline bodies, applied to repeated office or out-of-office measurements. It is a condition of sustained hemodynamic stress rather than a single number on one visit.
Primary (essential) hypertension dominates epidemiologically; secondary causes exist and are searched when clues appear.
Cardiovascular risk scales integrate hypertension with lipids, smoking, diabetes, and organ damage markers.
Misconception: feeling well excludes hypertension. Most people are asymptomatic for years.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Elevated pressure increases arterial wall shear and promotes endothelial dysfunction. Stiffening reduces compliance, raising systolic pressure and pulse wave reflection.
Left ventricular hypertrophy develops as the heart adapts to afterload; diastolic dysfunction and HFpEF pathways follow.
Microvascular kidney injury and retinal changes reflect chronic end-organ exposure.
Hypertensive emergencies and urgencies represent extreme pressure with or without acute organ dysfunction-distinct teaching categories with protocol care.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Headache alone is a poor screening symptom. Severe hypertension may present with dyspnea from heart failure or neurologic symptoms when end organs acutely fail.
Secondary hypertension clues: young age, resistant HTN, hypokalemia, abdominal bruit, snoring with daytime sleepiness.
Orthostatic symptoms may relate to overtreatment in older adults-balance matters.
Student drill: List four silent end-organ consequences of chronic hypertension.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Office BP with proper technique, home monitoring, and ambulatory BP refine diagnosis. Labs evaluate renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lipids.
ECG and urinalysis screen for LVH and kidney involvement. Echocardiography quantifies hypertrophy when management decisions benefit.
Secondary workup (aldosterone, renal imaging, sleep study) follows selective triggers.
Target organ assessment informs risk, not just the BP number.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Memorize major drug classes by mechanism: RAAS blockade, calcium channel blockade, thiazide-like diuretics, beta blockade where indicated-not as first-line for all in modern guidelines.
Practice lifestyle counseling themes: sodium reduction, activity, weight, alcohol moderation.
Study hypertension in pregnancy separately-overlapping but distinct disorders.
Use phenotyping language: white coat, masked, resistant-without self-diagnosis.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Hypertension education links invisible pressure load to visible end-organ change over years. Measurement rigor and repeated readings define the diagnosis.
Mechanisms span vessels, heart, kidney, and brain-consistent with its role as a root risk factor for many Cardily topics.
Cardily teaches biology and evaluation; medication choices require clinicians who know your full risk picture.

takeaways: White coat hypertension is elevated blood pressure in medical settings with lower readings elsewhere.
Measurement context and anxiety physiology explain part of the pattern; device and technique still matter.
Some individuals with white coat patterns develop sustained hypertension over time-longitudinal follow-up themes appear in studies.
Out-of-office monitoring confirms phenotyping before labeling.
Treatment is not automatic; decisions integrate overall cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: White coat hypertension describes a blood pressure phenotype where clinic readings exceed ambulatory or home averages. The ‘white coat’ metaphor captures medical environment stress, though not every patient feels anxious consciously.
Why it matters: overtreatment from clinic-only highs and undertreatment if masked components coexist are both risks when phenotyping is skipped.
Automated office blood pressure (multiple readings unattended) reduces but may not eliminate the effect.
Misconception: white coat means no action ever. Risk integration still applies.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Sympathetic activation in clinical encounters can transiently raise cardiac output and vascular tone. Repeated clinic visits may show variable spikes.
Long-term organ damage risk in pure white coat appears lower than sustained hypertension in many cohorts, yet not zero-debate continues on aggressiveness of follow-up.
Progression to sustained hypertension is a reason for periodic ambulatory monitoring in teaching plans.
Evidence humility: definitions and thresholds evolve; avoid rigid lifetime labels without re-testing.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate white coat from poor technique (cuff too small, talking during measurement) and from true sustained hypertension using ABPM or structured home logs.
Masked hypertension may coexist in some individuals-office normal, out-of-office high-opposite pattern worth excluding.
Secondary hypertension should still be considered when clues appear regardless of white coat label.
Student drill: Design a monitoring plan conceptually for discordant office and home readings.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Lifestyle modification benefits almost all blood pressure phenotypes at population level.
Pharmacologic treatment decisions weigh global risk, end-organ damage, and patient preference when ambulatory averages borderline.
Some guidelines suggest treatment for high-risk profiles even with white coat pattern-read primary sources for nuance.
Behavioral interventions to reduce measurement anxiety are adjuncts, not replacements for objective monitoring.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Discuss health literacy when teaching home BP-teach back method.
Explore disparities: who gets ABPM access in your community?
Ask preceptors how they document phenotyping in charts.
Review medicolegal themes when dismissing clinic highs without out-of-office data.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: White coat hypertension teaches that context shapes numbers. Medical environments are not neutral measurement chambers.
Confirmatory out-of-office profiles protect against misclassification and guide follow-up intensity.
Cardily emphasizes measurement science; treatment belongs to shared decisions with your clinician.

takeaways: Resistant hypertension is generally defined as blood pressure above goal despite three antihypertensive agents including a diuretic at adequate doses-exact criteria follow current guidelines.
Pseudo-resistance from poor adherence, white coat effect, or incorrect measurement is common and should be excluded.
Secondary causes become more likely in resistant cases educationally.
Spironolactone often appears in add-on therapy trials for true resistance-class-level teaching.
Specialist referral and structured workup are typical themes.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Resistant hypertension labels persistently elevated blood pressure despite lifestyle measures and pharmacologic therapy from multiple classes, including a diuretic, when doses are optimized and adherence confirmed.
Definitions used in trials and guidelines give learners a common language for epidemiology and therapy research.
Not every ‘hard to treat’ patient meets formal resistance criteria-precision prevents nihilism.
Misconception: resistance equals renal artery stenosis. Many cases remain multifactorial essential hypertension.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Volume expansion from inadequate diuretic effect or high sodium intake sustains pressure despite RAAS blockade.
Sleep apnea, obesity, alcohol, and NSAIDs antagonize control-modifiable contributors belong on every resistant checklist.
Secondary aldosteronism and primary hyperaldosteronism elevate resistance prevalence in specialty series.
Arterial stiffness in older adults limits diastolic lowering even with multiple agents.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Resistant hypertension rarely announces itself with unique symptoms; headaches or epistaxis are not reliable markers.
Hypokalemia or muscle cramps may hint at aldosterone excess in secondary forms.
Snoring and daytime somnolence suggest sleep apnea as contributor.
Medication side effects (ankle swelling from calcium channel blockers) affect adherence-ask sensitively.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: ABPM or home BP confirms true resistance versus white coat or masked patterns.
Labs: renal function, electrolytes, aldosterone-renin ratio when indicated, urinalysis.
Imaging for renal artery stenosis selectively-not universal screening.
Adherence testing (pharmacy fills, observed ingestion) is pragmatic before invasive workups.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: List pseudo-resistance causes before accepting the resistant label.
Study PATHWAY-2 style narratives about spironolactone add-on qualitatively.
Learn renal denervation as evolving option with mixed trial history-evidence humility.
Practice explaining multidrug regimens with mechanism-based rationales to simulated patients.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Resistant hypertension is a guideline-defined phenotype after adherence and measurement are verified. Volume and secondary drivers dominate teaching differentials.
Workup escalates thoughtfully toward sleep apnea, aldosterone, and vascular causes when clues align.
Cardily clarifies terminology; tuning therapy requires clinicians managing your full medication list.

takeaways: Secondary hypertension arises from identifiable causes-renal, endocrine, vascular, obstructive sleep apnea, drugs-rather than idiopathic essential mechanisms alone.
Clues include early onset, resistant HTN, hypokalemia, abdominal bruit, and episodic symptoms in pheochromocytoma.
Primary aldosteronism is more common than classic teaching once suggested-screening themes expanded in modern guidelines.
Treating the cause may cure or greatly improve pressure control.
Not every patient needs exhaustive secondary workup-risk-based selection preserves efficiency.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: Secondary hypertension means elevated blood pressure driven by a specific disease process amenable to targeted therapy. It represents a minority of all hypertension but a larger share of resistant or young-onset cases.
Why diagnosis matters: stenting renal artery stenosis, removing adrenal adenoma, or treating apnea can transform control and reduce cardiovascular risk.
Essential hypertension remains the default diagnosis after appropriate screening negatives.
Misconception: secondary workup is only for exotic cases-sleep apnea and primary aldosteronism are common in specialty practice.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Renal parenchymal disease reduces sodium excretion; renovascular disease activates RAAS via ischemic kidney.
Primary hyperaldosteronism causes sodium retention and potassium wasting. Pheochromocytoma secretes catecholamine surges with paroxysmal hypertension.
Cushing syndrome, thyroid extremes, and acromegaly alter pressure through volume and vascular tone.
Coarctation of the aorta presents in youth with arm-leg BP gradients and rib notching on imaging in classic descriptions.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous hypokalemia, adrenal incidentaloma, or family history of early stroke prompts aldosteronism screening in guidelines.
Episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations suggest pheochromocytoma-plasma or urine metanephrines in workup pathways.
Snoring and obesity redirect toward sleep apnea evaluation.
Medication and substance review catches NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, liquorice, and immunosuppressants.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Treatment targets underlying cause: adrenalectomy or mineralocorticoid antagonists for aldosteronism, revascularization or medical RAAS blockade for renovascular disease depending on anatomy and kidney function.
OSA therapy with positive airway pressure may lower BP modestly but improves overall risk.
Beta blockade precedes alpha blockade in pheochromocytoma preparation in teaching sequences-protocol detail for specialists.
Coarctation repair in suitable anatomy reduces afterload long term.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Build an age-based secondary HTN differential: pediatric coarctation versus adult renal disease.
Practice interpreting aldosterone-renin ratio limitations with common medications.
Study when to image renal arteries noninvasively.
Maintain skepticism about ‘rule-out’ lists-follow-up matters if clinical course worsens.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Secondary hypertension rewards curiosity when blood pressure behaves unexpectedly. Clues in age, labs, and history steer efficient testing.
Mechanisms tie to renal, adrenal, vascular, and sleep pathways already familiar from other Cardily articles.
Cardily teaches when to think secondary; confirmatory testing and treatment are clinician-led.

takeaways: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) features recurrent upper airway collapse during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges.
Cardiovascular links include hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension in observational and interventional frameworks.
Daytime sleepiness and witnessed apneas are history clues; polysomnography confirms diagnosis.
Positive airway pressure is first-line therapy in many guidelines; adherence challenges are real.
Treating OSA complements but does not replace standard heart failure and AF therapies.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: Sleep apnea disrupts normal nocturnal physiology: repeated obstructions raise intrathoracic pressure swings, activate sympathetic tone, and drop oxygen saturation. The heart experiences cyclic stress akin to many brief insults nightly.
Why cardiologists care: OSA clusters with obesity, hypertension, and AF-conditions already on ward rounds daily.
Central sleep apnea appears in heart failure with Cheyne-Stokes respiration-a related but distinct physiology.
Misconception: only obese men have OSA. Thin patients and women are under-recognized.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Intermittent hypoxia promotes oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction. Sympathetic activation elevates nocturnal and daytime blood pressure.
Transmural pressure swings affect atria and ventricles, potentially promoting remodeling and arrhythmia substrates.
Pulmonary vasoconstriction during hypoxemia contributes to pulmonary hypertension in severe disease over time.
Mechanistic proof in humans is complex; observational data dominate much of the literature-evidence humility applies.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate fatigue from depression, hypothyroidism, and sedating medications. Questionnaires (STOP-BANG) support screening but do not diagnose.
Insomnia and sleep deprivation mimic some symptoms without apneas.
Central apnea in HF requires distinguishing obstructive component before device choices.
Student drill: Link each symptom cluster to either OSA or left HF decompensation thoughtfully.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: CPAP reduces apneas and improves sleep quality; blood pressure and AF burden may improve in trials subsets.
Weight loss and positional therapy are adjuncts. Mandibular devices help mild OSA in selected patients.
In treatment-resistant hypertension, screening for OSA is guideline-highlighted.
Adaptive servo-ventilation has specific cautions in certain HF populations-learners read trial safety signals.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Ask how sleep studies are accessed in your health system equitably.
Discuss adherence coaching for CPAP as part of cardiovascular care teams.
Explore bidirectional screening: new AF patients referred for sleep evaluation rates.
Review ethical marketing of home sleep tests versus full polysomnography.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Sleep apnea and the heart intersect through nightly hypoxia, pressure swings, and sympathetic activation-mechanisms that amplify common cardiac conditions.
Diagnosis requires sleep testing; cardiovascular benefit from treatment is plausible and supported in parts of the literature with ongoing study.
Cardily connects sleep physiology to cardiology wards; CPAP prescriptions and follow-up belong to sleep and primary teams coordinating with cardiology.

takeaways: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy include chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and eclampsia-each with distinct timing and implications.
Preeclampsia features new hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction after twenty weeks gestation in classic teaching.
Placental malperfusion and angiogenic imbalance models explain much of pathophysiology research.
Maternal and fetal risks drive close monitoring; delivery timing is a core management theme in obstetric cardiology interfaces.
Long-term cardiovascular risk rises after preeclampsia-surveillance themes postpartum appear in prevention discussions.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: Pregnancy-associated hypertension spans conditions where blood pressure elevation occurs in relation to gestation. Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy or appears before twenty weeks; gestational hypertension arises later without preeclampsia features initially.
Preeclampsia adds multisystem involvement-renal, hepatic, neurologic, hematologic-beyond pressure alone.
Eclampsia denotes seizures superimposed on preeclampsia spectrum.
Misconception: mild BP rise in pregnancy is always benign. Context and trajectory matter.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Abnormal placentation with deficient spiral artery remodeling reduces perfusion, releasing anti-angiogenic factors that injure endothelium systemically.
Endothelial dysfunction causes hypertension, proteinuria, and organ edema. HELLP syndrome represents hematologic and hepatic severe end of spectrum.
Cardiac strain may produce diastolic dysfunction or peripartum cardiomyopathy overlap in severe cases.
Fetal growth restriction reflects placental insufficiency parallel to maternal symptoms.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate preeclampsia from gestational hypertension when proteinuria or organ dysfunction emerges.
Mimics include thrombotic microangiopathies and acute fatty liver-high-acuity differentials in specialty care.
Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia complicates labeling when baseline pressure already elevated.
Student drill: List maternal organ systems involved in severe preeclampsia beyond kidneys.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Antihypertensive choices in pregnancy differ from standard adult lists-certain agents contraindicated, others preferred in guideline tables learners consult.
Magnesium sulfate prevents eclampsia in severe preeclampsia protocols.
Delivery is definitive for preeclampsia when maternal or fetal stability requires-timing individualized.
Postpartum BP can surge; long-term CVD prevention counseling follows many societies’ recommendations qualitatively.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: How do cardiology consults participate in severe preeclampsia with pulmonary edema?
When is echocardiography ordered in hypertensive pregnancy teaching cases?
How are racial disparities in maternal morbidity addressed in your curriculum?
What postpartum follow-up intervals are taught for BP and risk factor screening?

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Pregnancy-associated hypertension unites obstetrics and cardiovascular pathophysiology through placental perfusion and endothelial injury.
Classification by timing and organ involvement guides monitoring and delivery decisions-always specialist territory.
Cardily educates on mechanisms and long-term risk themes; prenatal care teams manage individual pregnancies.

takeaways: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step in hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
Lower intracellular cholesterol upregulates LDL receptors, clearing LDL particles from blood.
Pleiotropic effects on inflammation and endothelium are discussed but LDL lowering remains primary proven mechanism for ASCVD risk reduction.
Muscle symptoms are reported and evaluated clinically; true statin intolerance rates are debated.
Statins are a class with varying potency and drug interactions-prescribing is clinician role.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Statins are lipid-lowering medications widely used in primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Mechanism teaching starts at the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
By blocking mevalonate production, hepatocytes sense cholesterol depletion and increase surface LDL receptors, pulling LDL from circulation.
Non-statin therapies exist, but statins anchor evidence from major outcome trials learners encounter in coursework.
Misconception: statins only help if diet is ignored. Lifestyle remains foundational alongside pharmacotherapy in guidelines.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Reduced LDL particle concentration slows atherosclerosis progression in imaging and event trials conceptually.
Some statins stabilize plaque biology in research models through anti-inflammatory pathways independent of LDL-extent of clinical contribution remains secondary to LDL lowering in most teaching.
Hepatic synthesis inhibition also reduces VLDL production indirectly in some agents.
Genetic variants affecting statin transport (SLCO1B1) inform myopathy risk discussions in precision medicine contexts.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Statins do not typically cause hypertension symptoms; muscle aching is the common patient concern in education.
Severe muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) is rare; learners recognize when urgent evaluation themes appear in protocols.
Liver enzyme elevation can occur; monitoring practices follow guideline schedules.
New-onset diabetes risk is slightly increased in some populations-a risk-benefit theme in long-term prevention.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Lipid panels measure LDL-C, sometimes apoB or LDL particle number in advanced labs.
Baseline and follow-up liver tests appear in protocol summaries.
Coronary calcium and imaging endpoints appear in research, not routine statin monitoring for every patient.
Drug interaction review (CYP pathways, fibrates) is pharmacy-collaborative skill.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Draw cholesterol synthesis pathway with statin block point.
Compare intensity tiers (low, moderate, high) conceptually without dosing numbers here.
Study primary versus secondary prevention trial populations separately.
Practice shared decision conversations about benefit and muscle symptom reporting.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Statins teach enzymology linked to public health: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition lowers LDL through receptor upregulation.
Symptom monitoring and interaction awareness belong to longitudinal prescribing relationships.
Cardily explains mechanisms for learners; whether and which statin fits you is a clinician decision with your lipid profile and history.

takeaways: SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption, causing glycosuria and modest glucose lowering in diabetes.
Heart failure trials showed benefit in HFrEF and broader HF populations beyond glucose effects, reshaping cardiology conversations.
Proposed mechanisms include natriuresis, reduced preload, metabolic shifts, and effects on myocardial energetics-active research area.
They are not interchangeable with GLP-1 agents though both appear in cardiometabolic guidelines for different indications.
Euglycemic DKA and genital infections are teaching safety topics in appropriate populations.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors were developed as diabetes drugs targeting proximal tubule glucose reabsorption. Unexpected cardiovascular and renal outcome benefits in large trials redirected attention to heart failure therapeutics.
Why HF care changed: benefits appeared relatively independent of baseline diabetes in key heart failure trials, prompting guideline additions for selected HF patients.
Drug names end in -flozin in many markets-class recognition for students.
Misconception: SGLT2 inhibitors are ‘only diabetes pills.’ Their HF indications stand alone educationally.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Glycosuria osmotically diureses sodium and water, lowering preload and blood pressure modestly.
Shift toward ketone body utilization in myocardium is hypothesized to improve efficiency during stress-human proof evolving.
Reduced interstitial congestion and improved ventricular loading conditions may explain symptomatic HF improvements.
Renal hemodynamic effects (afferent arteriole modulation in models) contribute to kidney outcome trials.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate SGLT2 use for HF versus glycemic control indications on labels, which evolve by region.
Contraindications include hypersensitivity and, in some settings, type 1 diabetes due to DKA risk themes.
Volume depletion symptoms may appear early-clinical monitoring is standard.
Student drill: Why might loop diuretic doses change when SGLT2 inhibitors start in HF teaching cases?

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Initiation in stabilized HF patients appears in protocol education; acute sick-day rules differ from maintenance.
Combination with ARNI, beta blockers, MRA, and other GDMT is common in trial populations learners read about.
Renal function monitoring follows product labels and local guidance.
Cost and access disparities affect real-world uptake-health systems topic.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Track EMPEROR, DAPA-HF trial narratives qualitatively in coursework.
Discuss cardiorenal syndrome patients who qualify for multiple protective agents.
Explore patient counseling on genital hygiene and infection recognition educationally.
Review sick-day medication lists in diabetes versus HF contexts.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: SGLT2 inhibitors illustrate how diabetes therapeutics crossed into heart failure through robust outcome trials.
Mechanisms likely combine hemodynamic and metabolic effects; research continues refining models.
Cardily teaches class concepts; starting or stopping these drugs is for prescribers managing your conditions.

takeaways: Atrial thrombus most often forms in the left atrial appendage during atrial fibrillation with stasis.
Thromboembolism to brain causes ischemic stroke; systemic emboli also occur.
Transesophageal echocardiography detects appendage thrombus before cardioversion in many protocols.
Anticoagulation reduces stroke risk based on risk scores; left atrial appendage occlusion devices are alternatives in selected patients.
Not all AF strokes imply visible thrombus on a single study-emboli may have already departed.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Atrial thrombus is organized clot within the atrium, classically in the left atrial appendage-a blind-ended pouch with low flow during fibrillation.
Stroke pathway: thrombus dislodges, travels through systemic circulation, lodges in cerebral artery producing ischemic infarct.
Teaching ties together AF, stasis (Virchow’s triad), and anticoagulation rationale.
Misconception: brief AF episodes never cause stroke. Burden and risk factors integrate in scores.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Loss of organized atrial contraction during AF reduces appendage emptying. Endothelial injury and procoagulant milieu complete Virchow elements.
Large anterior MI with apical akinesis can produce ventricular thrombus-different chamber, similar embolic stroke risk theme.
Mechanical valves and endocarditis vegetations are additional cardioembolic sources learners list alongside appendage thrombus.
Appendage morphology (chicken wing versus cauliflower) appears in occlusion device planning research.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Ischemic stroke symptoms prompt urgent neuroimaging; AF may be newly diagnosed during workup.
Silent AF on extended monitoring explains some cryptogenic strokes retrospectively.
TIA with AF warrants anticoagulation discussions unless bleeding contraindications dominate.
Student drill: Connect CHA2DS2-VASc components to pathophysiology, not memorization alone.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: TEE visualizes appendage before elective cardioversion when AF duration exceeds guideline thresholds.
Anticoagulation with DOACs or warfarin per scores; LAA closure for eligible patients intolerant of long-term anticoagulation in selected centers.
Cardioversion without adequate anticoagulation risks dislodging pre-existing thrombus-protocol timing matters.
Post-stroke anticoagulation start timing balances hemorrhagic transformation risk-neurology-led.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Compare warfarin INR monitoring with DOAC predictable pharmacology at class level.
Study Watchman and similar devices as mechanical appendage exclusion conceptually.
Review bleeding risk scores alongside stroke scores in shared decisions.
Practice explaining why aspirin alone is insufficient for many AF stroke prevention scenarios historically.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Atrial thrombus and stroke education links AF stasis in the appendage to embolic brain infarction.
Imaging and anticoagulation frameworks reduce-but do not eliminate-cardioembolic events.
Cardily clarifies pathways; anticoagulation choices require individualized clinical judgment.

takeaways: Coronary artery ectasia is abnormal arterial dilation exceeding adjacent normal segments, sometimes involving aneurysmal segments.
Atherosclerosis, connective tissue disorders, and vasculitis appear in etiology lists.
Slow flow and thrombosis risk are teaching concerns in dilated segments.
Angiography defines ectasia; management often mirrors CAD plus antithrombotic considerations in specialty guidance.
Ectasia differs from fistula and from normal variant mild tortuosity.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Coronary ectasia describes segments of coronary artery that are dilated rather than narrowed. When dilation exceeds defined proportions of neighboring artery, angiographic reports label ectasia or aneurysm.
It may coexist with stenoses in the same vessel, creating mixed disease physiology.
Less common than typical CAD alone, ectasia appears in registries and case series learners skim for patterns.
Misconception: ectasia is harmless dilated pipe. Flow stagnation can promote thrombosis.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Atherosclerotic remodeling sometimes produces expansive rather than constrictive plaque phenotype.
Kawasaki disease history in youth connects to adult aneurysmal coronaries in some populations.
Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos associations remind clinicians to think connective tissue when multiple ectatic vessels appear.
Turbulent slow flow may cause ischemic symptoms despite absent critical stenosis.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Chest pain may mimic angina from slow flow or thrombotic episodes.
Acute coronary syndromes can occur with thrombosis in ectatic segments.
Symptoms do not correlate linearly with degree of dilation.
Student drill: Differentiate ectasia from coronary fistula shunting physiology.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Coronary angiography remains reference; CTA also depicts ectasia.
Functional testing may reveal ischemia when slow flow suspected.
Antiplatelet therapy themes appear in case-based reviews; anticoagulation considered when thrombotic history-specialist decisions.
Revascularization stenting of ectatic segments carries technical challenges; medical management often dominates.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Search for systemic vasculitis or connective tissue stigmata when ectasia is diffuse.
Study Kawasaki long-term follow-up guidelines in pediatric-to-adult transition clinics.
Compare ectasia prevalence reports cautiously across eras of imaging sensitivity.
Document family history of aneurysmal disease when present.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Coronary artery ectasia expands the coronary phenotype library beyond stenosis-only thinking.
Mechanisms blend atherosclerosis, inflammation, and structural weakness with slow-flow ischemia.
Cardily educates on recognition; antithrombotic and procedural strategies belong to imaging-informed specialists.

takeaways: Coronary fistulas are abnormal connections between coronary arteries and cardiac chambers or great vessels.
Most are congenital; some acquired after trauma or procedures.
Left-to-right or coronary steal physiology may cause ischemia, volume load, or heart failure.
Small fistulas may be observed; large shunts may need closure via catheter or surgery.
Continuous murmur and dilated coronary on echo/CT raise suspicion.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: A coronary fistula bypasses the myocardial capillary bed, connecting a coronary artery directly to a low-pressure chamber or vessel. Shunt direction and magnitude determine hemodynamic impact.
Congenital fistulas are often diagnosed in childhood but may present later with arrhythmia or heart failure.
Multiple fistulas and associated anomalies appear in complex congenital heart curricula.
Misconception: all fistulas require immediate closure. Tiny fistulas may be incidental.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Coronary steal during increased myocardial demand diverts flow away from capillaries, provoking ischemia in theory.
Chronic left-to-right shunt into right heart chambers loads volume and can dilate chambers.
Endocarditis risk at fistula entry sites is a rare teaching point.
Arrhythmias may arise from adjacent myocardial irritation or chamber dilation.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate fistula from anomalous origin, bridging, and patent ductus arteriosus murmurs.
Heart failure symptoms, exercise intolerance, or angina prompt quantification of shunt.
In adults, new fistula after chest trauma or biopsy is acquired differential.
Student drill: Explain why a continuous murmur suggests fistula versus stenotic systolic murmur.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Echocardiography may show dilated coronary arteries; CT or MRI angiography maps course.
Catheter closure with coils or plugs is option for hemodynamically significant fistulas in expert centers.
Surgical ligation remains for complex anatomy.
Follow-up imaging confirms closure and monitors for recurrence.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Review congenital heart transition clinics where adult fistulas are re-discovered.
Discuss radiation planning for interventional closure educationally.
Explore Qp:Qs shunt concepts linking to other left-to-right lesions.
Practice counseling parents when pediatric incidental fistula is found.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Coronary fistulas teach abnormal connections and shunt physiology within the coronary circuit.
Symptoms track steal and volume load severity; small lesions may stay quiescent.
Cardily maps anatomy and hemodynamics; closure decisions require quantitative imaging and experienced operators.

takeaways: Left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) features prominent trabeculations and deep intertrabecular recesses on imaging.
It is controversial: distinguishing pathologic noncompaction from normal variant trabeculation challenges diagnosis.
Associations include heart failure, arrhythmia, and thromboembolism in case series.
Genetic cardiomyopathy overlap exists; family screening themes appear in specialty clinics.
Criteria based on trabecular-to-compact layer ratios differ by modality-humility in labeling.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: LVNC is described as failure of myocardial compaction during embryogenesis, leaving excessive trabecular meshwork. Imaging reports increasingly mention noncompaction in diverse patients, fueling diagnostic debate.
Why controversy matters: overdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary device therapy or family testing; underdiagnosis may miss true cardiomyopathy.
Some view LVNC as morphologic expression shared by other cardiomyopathies rather than standalone disease.
Misconception: any trabeculations on echo equal LVNC. Athletes and Black individuals may have physiologic trabeculations.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Noncompacted myocardium may contract poorly, contributing to systolic dysfunction and heart failure symptoms.
Trabecular recesses can harbor thrombus in theory, raising anticoagulation discussions when EF low or AF present.
Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death reports appear in registries-risk stratification imperfect.
Genetic mutations overlap with dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy pathways.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Differentiate LVNC from HCM apical variant, apical aneurysm, and thrombus masquerading as trabeculations.
Contrast-enhanced MRI helps characterize trabecular structure and scar.
Symptoms mirror other cardiomyopathies: dyspnea, palpitations, syncope.
Student drill: List two imaging criteria sets and note they may disagree.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Heart failure therapy follows cardiomyopathy guidelines when dysfunction present.
ICD decisions use general sudden death risk tools with caution due to evolving LVNC risk data.
Anticoagulation not universal-tied to AF, thrombus, or very low EF per clinician judgment.
Genetic counseling offered when familial disease suspected.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Read skepticism literature alongside advocacy patient stories for balanced view.
Study athlete hearts to avoid mislabeling physiologic trabeculations.
Document serial imaging when diagnosis uncertain rather than rushing labels.
Explore registries contributing to refined criteria over time.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Myocardial noncompaction sits at the intersection of embryology, imaging technology, and cardiomyopathy genetics-with legitimate diagnostic controversy.
When dysfunction or arrhythmia exists, management aligns with heart failure and sudden death prevention principles regardless of label debates.
Cardily encourages nuanced reading of imaging reports; definitive diagnosis often needs expert echo/MRI correlation.

takeaways: High-output heart failure features elevated cardiac output yet inadequate organ perfusion because of extremely low systemic vascular resistance or metabolic demand.
Causes include severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, arteriovenous fistulas, beriberi, and pregnancy hyperdynamic states.
Ejection fraction may be normal or high; classic low-EF heart failure frameworks mislead if output is not measured conceptually.
Treat underlying cause often reverses failure-volume and afterload management adjunctive.
Warm extremities and wide pulse pressure are exam teaching clues.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: High-output heart failure is heart failure syndrome with increased cardiac output meeting defined hemodynamic thresholds on catheterization in classic descriptions, yet patients experience congestion and hypoperfusion symptoms because vascular beds are massively dilated or metabolic needs outstrip delivery.
It contradicts beginner assumption that heart failure always means low output numerically.
Recognition prevents mislabeling as primary cardiomyopathy when the driver is thyroid storm or fistula.
Misconception: normal EF excludes heart failure entirely-high-output HF is counterexample.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Anemia forces increased cardiac output to maintain oxygen delivery; chronic high flow dilates chambers.
Thyrotoxicosis raises contractility and heart rate while dropping SVR.
Large AV fistulas shunt blood, increasing venous return and output until heart decompensates.
Beriberi from thiamine deficiency causes vasodilation and high-output failure in nutritional teaching cases.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Warm flushed skin, bounding pulses, and tachycardia contrast with cold low-output failure.
Hyperdynamic precordium on exam and wide pulse pressure support teaching diagnosis before labs return.
Pregnancy normally increases output; peripartum cardiomyopathy is different entity-avoid conflation.
Student drill: Given anemia and dyspnea, list findings favoring high-output HF versus iron deficiency alone.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Echocardiography may show hyperdynamic function and chamber dilation.
Right heart catheterization confirms high output and low SVR when invasive assessment done.
Labs: CBC, thyroid function, thiamine in appropriate contexts.
Treat cause: transfuse or replete iron thoughtfully, treat hyperthyroidism, close fistula surgically or intervene.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Link obstetric hyperdynamic physiology to cardiomyopathy red flags separately in notes.
Study Paget disease bone hypervascularity as rare high-output cause in textbooks.
Practice hemodynamic vocabulary: CO, SVR, PVR, wedge pressures.
Review diuretic use when congestion persists after cause treated.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: High-output heart failure teaches that syndrome definition is about adequacy of perfusion relative to need, not output number alone.
Underlying shunts, hormones, and anemia explain most cases-fix the driver when possible.
Cardily highlights exam and hemodynamic clues; invasive confirmation and cause-specific treatment stay in clinical teams’ hands.

takeaways: Low-output heart failure emphasizes inadequate forward flow and perfusion, often with cool extremities and hypotension.
Profiles overlap with ‘cold and wet’ or ‘cold and dry’ congestion-perfusion grids used in acute care teaching.
Cardiac index and lactate conceptually reflect perfusion; echocardiography shows weak squeeze in many cases.
Inotropes and mechanical support appear in advanced decompensation protocols-not self-directed therapies.
Differentiate from distributive shock where output may be high initially.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: Low-output signs appear when the heart cannot generate sufficient stroke volume to perfuse organs despite often elevated filling pressures. Patients may be congested, underperfused, or both-the ‘cold’ descriptor signals vasoconstriction and reduced extremity flow.
Why it matters: therapy differs from hypertensive flash pulmonary edema where afterload reduction dominates without hypotension.
Low output occurs in HFrEF decompensation, massive PE, tamponade, and severe valvular disease among other causes.
Misconception: all decompensated HF patients have high blood pressure. Some present in cardiogenic shock.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Reduced forward flow activates sympathetic and renin responses, raising vasoconstriction at cost of end-organ perfusion.
Renal hypoperfusion causes oliguria; gut ischemia causes pain and malabsorption in extreme cases.
Lactic acidosis in advanced shock reflects anaerobic metabolism-emergency medicine crossover.
Ventricular interdependence means RV failure can reduce LV filling, lowering output further.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate cardiogenic shock from sepsis and hemorrhagic shock using exam, echo, and invasive pressures when available.
Tamponade and tension pneumothorax are reversible mechanical causes of low output-always on emergency differentials.
Large pulmonary embolism reduces LV preload abruptly.
Student drill: Place tamponade, PE, and MI shock on a perfusion-congestion grid.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) increase contractility in selected hospitalized patients under monitoring.
Vasopressors may maintain coronary perfusion pressure when hypotensive.
Mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, ECMO themes) bridges to recovery or transplant in advanced centers.
Diuretics cautiously when profoundly hypotensive-preload dependence varies.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Study SCAI shock stages as organizational framework in some curricula.
Discuss ethics of escalation versus palliation in recurrent cardiogenic shock.
Review lactate clearance as resuscitation marker conceptually.
Practice ultrasound skills assessing IVC and ventricular function at bedside educationally.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Low-output heart failure signs orient learners to perfusion failure-not only lung congestion.
Cold extremities, hypotension, and organ dysfunction prompt wide differential before defaulting to one diagnosis.
Cardily teaches frameworks like cold/wet profiles; vasoactive and mechanical therapies belong in monitored critical care settings.

takeaways: WHO pulmonary hypertension groups classify hemodynamic etiologies: PAH (1), left heart disease (2), lung disease/hypoxia (3), CTEPH (4), unclear/multifactorial (5).
Group determines therapy-PAH drugs are not for all pulmonary hypertension.
Right heart catheterization with wedge pressure and PVR defines groups formally.
Echo estimates pulmonary pressures but cannot alone assign group.
Classification literacy prevents treatment errors and anchors research enrollment.

sections.heading: Why this diagnosis matters
paragraphs: Pulmonary hypertension is elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure on hemodynamic testing. The WHO grouping separates mechanisms so clinicians choose appropriate pathways.
Group 1 PAH is pre-capillary with elevated PVR; Group 2 reflects post-capillary elevation from left heart failure or valvular disease with wedge pressure context.
Group 3 arises from chronic lung disease and hypoxia; Group 4 from chronic thromboembolic obstruction amenable sometimes to surgery.
Misconception: one ‘pulmonary hypertension pill’ treats all groups.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and natural history
paragraphs: Left heart disease elevates pulmonary venous pressure, eventually remodeling arterioles secondarily.
Hypoxic vasoconstriction in COPD or sleep apnea chronically raises pressures.
Unresolved emboli organize into chronic obstructions raising PVR in CTEPH.
Group 5 captures multifactorial or unclear cases like hematologic disorders.

sections.heading: Differential thinking
paragraphs: Differentiate PAH from pulmonary venous hypertension due to mitral stenosis using wedge and waveforms.
Screen CTEPH with V/Q scan in guideline teaching when PH unexplained.
Connect systemic sclerosis to PAH subset in rheumatology-cardiology overlap.
Student drill: Assign example patients to groups before seeing cath data, then revise after.

sections.heading: Treatment categories at a high level
paragraphs: Group 1 therapies: endothelin antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclins, sGC stimulators in combinations.
Group 2: treat left heart failure, valves, ischemia-not PAH vasodilators alone.
Group 3: oxygen, lung disease management; PAH drugs generally avoided.
Group 4: pulmonary thromboendarterectomy or balloon angioplasty in expert centers when operable.

sections.heading: How to keep learning responsibly
paragraphs: Memorize group numbers with anchor examples, not exhaustive lists initially.
Follow world symposium updates when classifications refine subgroups.
Discuss access to PH specialty centers regionally.
Study exercise limitation as shared symptom across groups with different fixes.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Pulmonary hypertension groups organize a heterogeneous pressure elevation syndrome by mechanism.
Catheter hemodynamics plus clinical context assign group; echo alone is insufficient for therapy class choice.
Cardily builds classification literacy; PH centers manage vasoactive regimens and operability assessments.

takeaways: Frailty describes decreased physiologic reserve and vulnerability to stressors-common in older heart failure patients.
Frailty metrics predict hospitalization and mortality sometimes beyond ejection fraction alone.
Polypharmacy, sarcopenia, cognitive impairment, and slow gait intertwine with HF care.
Rehabilitation and nutritional support are multidisciplinary themes.
Advanced HF therapies (transplant, LVAD) may be limited by frailty assessments in programs.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Frailty is a geriatric syndrome of reduced reserve across multiple systems, not mere old age. Heart failure and frailty frequently coexist because shared risk factors and deconditioning loops reinforce each other.
Why function matters beyond EF: two patients with identical echo numbers may differ drastically in six-minute walk, hospitalization risk, and tolerance of uptitration.
Frailty indices (Fried phenotype, clinical frailty scale) standardize communication in research and some clinics.
Misconception: frailty means hospice-only care. Prehabilitation can improve trajectories in selected patients.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Chronic HF catabolic state promotes muscle wasting; low cardiac output limits activity, accelerating deconditioning.
Diuretics and dietary restrictions affect nutrition; gut congestion impairs absorption.
Anemia and kidney disease cluster with both frailty and HF.
Cognitive frailty complicates medication adherence and symptom reporting.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Differentiate frailty from depression, thyroid disease, and neurologic gait disorders.
Delirium during HF admission may unmask baseline cognitive frailty.
Orthostatic hypotension from polypharmacy causes falls-safety lens on rounds.
Student drill: List geriatric syndromes to assess on HF admission besides JVP.

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Cardiac rehab adapted to capacity improves strength when enrollment barriers addressed.
Medication simplification and deprescribing reviews reduce harm.
Palliative integration early for high-burden frail patients aligns with goals.
Transplant/LVAD programs use frailty screening to predict recovery-controversial thresholds evolve.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Observe how physical therapy documents gait speed in your hospital.
Discuss social determinants limiting rehab access.
Explore tele-rehab models post-COVID in curricula.
Ask how frailty changes GDMT uptitration pacing in elders.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Frailty and heart failure together remind learners that cardiovascular medicine is also functional medicine.
Reserve and resilience predict outcomes alongside pump metrics.
Cardily values holistic assessment; your care team should weigh function when setting goals and therapies.

takeaways: Pediatric hypertension uses age, sex, and height percentile-based thresholds-not adult cutoffs.
Primary hypertension links to obesity and family history; secondary causes are more common in younger children.
Coarctation, renal disease, and endocrine disorders appear in secondary differentials.
Ambulatory BP monitoring helps confirm diagnosis and assess nocturnal patterns.
Early recognition aims to prevent adult cardiovascular sequelae-long-view prevention theme.

sections.heading: Core definition
paragraphs: Hypertension in children and adolescents is defined by blood pressure readings above percentile tables adjusted for age, sex, and height. Adult numbers misapplied to children cause both over- and under-diagnosis.
Prevalence has risen with obesity epidemics, making BP measurement routine in well-child care education.
Staging (elevated, stage 1, stage 2) parallels adult concepts with pediatric tables.
Misconception: children do not get hypertension. They do, increasingly.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology in plain language
paragraphs: Obesity, insulin resistance, and sedentary behavior contribute to primary pediatric hypertension similar to adults.
Renal parenchymal disease dominates secondary causes in younger age groups.
Coarctation produces upper extremity hypertension with reduced lower extremity pulses in classic teaching.
Endocrine and medication causes mirror adult secondary lists at lower baseline prevalence.

sections.heading: Symptoms and warning patterns
paragraphs: Most pediatric hypertension is asymptomatic; headaches alone are weak screen.
Secondary clues: very young age, stage 2 without family history, hypokalemia, abdominal mass.
Sport participation questions arise when BP high-requires proper evaluation not automatic exclusion.
Student drill: Why measure leg BP when coarctation suspected?

sections.heading: Tests you will hear about
paragraphs: Repeated manual auscultatory measurement preferred in guidelines over casual oscillometric alone for diagnosis confirmation.
ABPM confirms persistence and nocturnal non-dipping.
Echocardiography for LV hypertrophy; labs and renal ultrasound in secondary workup pathways.
Lifestyle intervention first for many; pharmacotherapy follows guideline tables when indicated-pediatric specialist role.

sections.heading: Learning checkpoints
paragraphs: Study percentile charts interpretation in skills lab.
Compare US and European threshold nuances if training internationally.
Discuss school nurse BP screening limitations.
Explore transition to adult BP criteria around age eighteen in clinics.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Pediatric hypertension education centers percentile-based norms and higher secondary yield in the young.
Mechanisms bridge renal, vascular, and lifestyle factors with lifelong cardiovascular implications.
Cardily supports literacy for students crossing into adolescent medicine; diagnosis and treatment belong to pediatric clinicians.

takeaways: MINOCA (myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries) denotes MI criteria met with angiographic stenosis below obstructive thresholds.
Mechanisms include plaque rupture with non-obstructive disease, embolism, vasospasm, SCAD, and takotsubo.
Workup extends beyond angiography to MRI, OCT, provocative testing, and selective imaging in specialty pathways.
Prognosis varies by underlying cause-one label, multiple diseases.
Do not tell patients their arteries are ‘clean’ when troponin and clinical MI criteria are met.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: MINOCA describes patients who meet universal MI definitions-symptoms, biomarkers, ECG/imaging evidence-yet invasive angiography shows no obstructive atherosclerotic stenosis typically defined above seventy percent.
Why surprising angiograms matter: patients may feel dismissed if clinicians equate normal-looking arteries with ‘not a heart attack.’
MINOCA is common enough in registries to warrant structured evaluation algorithms in teaching hospitals.
Misconception: MINOCA is benign. Risk depends on identified mechanism.

sections.heading: How the heart and vessels are affected
paragraphs: Plaque disruption with distal embolization can cause infarction without focal severe stenosis on angiogram.
Coronary vasospasm and SCAD produce ischemia with non-atherosclerotic angiographic appearances.
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy mimics MI with troponin rise and wall motion abnormality.
Myocarditis enters differential when MRI shows subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement patterns.

sections.heading: How clinicians usually evaluate it
paragraphs: Repeat history for cocaine, stimulants, and extreme stress triggers.
Cardiac MRI clarifies infarct pattern versus myocarditis versus takotsubo ballooning.
Intracoronary imaging (OCT/IVUS) detects subtle plaque and dissection missed angiographically in expert hands.
Selective vasospasm testing reserved for specialty centers after stabilization.

sections.heading: What students should master first
paragraphs: Secondary prevention targets identified mechanism-statins if plaque present, avoid nitrates in some bridging cases per specialist, treat vasospasm if proven.
Antiplatelet duration follows MI guidelines unless alternative diagnosis changes plan.
Psychosocial support when takotsubo or SCAD in young patients.
Registry enrollment advances MINOCA science-students learn evolving field.

sections.heading: Questions for clinical conversations
paragraphs: Contrast MINOCA with INOCA (ischemia no obstructive CAD) symptom syndromes without infarction.
Practice explaining to simulated patient why further testing continues after ‘normal’ angiogram.
Study sex differences in MINOCA mechanisms in literature reviews.
Avoid anchoring on single negative test when clinical MI criteria satisfied.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: MINOCA teaches that myocardial infarction is a clinical-biomarker entity separable from angiographic stenosis severity.
Mechanistic workup transforms a confusing label into actionable categories like SCAD, spasm, or takotsubo.
Cardily promotes respect for patient experience when arteries look clear; definitive care paths need specialized evaluation.

takeaways: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is often inherited sarcomere protein disease with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy may cause dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
Symptoms include dyspnea, angina, syncope, and palpitations; sudden death risk stratification uses multiple markers.
Echocardiography with provocation (Valsalva, standing) assesses obstruction; MRI quantifies hypertrophy and scar.
Family screening with genetic testing when available is standard teaching theme.

sections.heading: What this condition is
paragraphs: HCM is defined by increased ventricular wall thickness not explained by loading conditions like hypertension or aortic stenosis alone. It is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in educational materials.
Genetic heterogeneity means family members may have varied expressivity-some hypertrophy, some genotype-positive phenotype-negative.
Apical, concentric, and septal patterns exist; obstruction is not universal.
Misconception: all HCM patients have murmur at rest. Obstruction can be labile.

sections.heading: How the heart and vessels are affected
paragraphs: Disorganized myocardial architecture causes diastolic dysfunction and arrhythmia substrate.
Dynamic obstruction from septal bulging and systolic anterior motion of mitral valve reduces outflow during exertion.
Microvascular ischemia contributes to angina despite clear epicardial coronaries.
Atrial fibrillation poorly tolerated when diastolic filling already impaired.

sections.heading: How clinicians usually evaluate it
paragraphs: Differentiate HCM from athlete’s heart (regression with deconditioning, normal diastolic function) and hypertension LVH.
Fabry disease and amyloidosis are infiltrative mimics in older appearing hypertrophy.
Aortic stenosis can coexist in elders-multiple problems possible.
Student drill: List echo features suggesting HCM versus athlete adaptation.

sections.heading: What students should master first
paragraphs: Beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers for symptoms; disopyramide in selected obstructive cases in specialty care.
Septal reduction therapy (myectomy or alcohol ablation) for refractory obstructive symptoms.
ICD for high-risk sudden death markers per guideline algorithms-specialist decision.
Sports restriction individualized after shared risk assessment-not one rule for all.

sections.heading: Questions for clinical conversations
paragraphs: Practice genetic counseling basics: autosomal dominant inheritance patterns.
Discuss cascade screening timelines for adolescent relatives.
Review contemporary athlete eligibility guidelines as evolving documents.
Explore patient advocacy organizations’ educational resources alongside textbooks.

sections.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy links genetics, asymmetric hypertrophy, dynamic obstruction, and arrhythmia risk into one teachable cardiomyopathy archetype.
Differentiating HCM from physiologic hypertrophy and infiltrative disease prevents misdiagnosis in both youth and elders.
Cardily explains concepts for learners; family screening, ICD decisions, and sports participation require HCM centers with full data.
